danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: I oktober 1805 besatte en russisk hær byerne og landsbyerne i ærkehertugdømmet Østrig, og nye regimenter, der ankom fra Rusland, slog lejr nær fæstningen Braunau og belastede de beboere, de blev indkvarteret hos. Braunau var hovedkvarter for øverstkommanderende Kutuzov.

Den 11. oktober 1805 havde et af de infanteriregimenter, der lige var nået Braunau, gjort holdt en halv mil fra byen for at vente på øverstbefalendes inspektion. Trods lokalitetens og omgivelsernes urussiske udseende — frugthaver, stenmure, tegltage og bakker i det fjerne — og trods at indbyggerne (der med nysgerrighed stirrede på soldaterne) ikke var russere, havde regimentet netop det udseende, som ethvert russisk regiment har, der forbereder sig til inspektion hvor som helst i hjertet af Rusland.

Aftenen før den sidste dagsmarch var der ankommet en ordre om, at den øverstbefalende ville inspicere regimentet på marchen. Selvom ordlyden ikke var klar for regimentschefen, og spørgsmålet opstod, om tropperne skulle være i marchuniform eller ej, blev det ved en rådgivning mellem bataljonscheferne besluttet at præsentere regimentet i paradeuniform ud fra det princip, at det altid er bedre at bukke for dybt end ikke dybt nok. Så soldaterne, der efter en march på tyve verst, holdt sig i gang hele natten med at lappe og pudse uden at lukke et øje, mens adjutanterne og kompagnicheferne regnede og kalkulerede, og om morgenen fremstod regimentet — i stedet for den omstrejfende, uordentlige flok, det havde været på gårsdagens march — som en velordnet opstilling af to tusind mand, der hver især kendte sin plads og sin pligt, havde hver knap og rem på plads og skinnede af renlighed. Og ikke blot var det ydre i orden — skulle den øverstbefalende behage at kigge under uniformerne, ville han på hver mand finde en ren skjorte og i hver tornyster det foreskrevne antal genstande — »syl, sæbe og det hele«, som soldaterne siger. Der var kun én omstændighed, ingen kunne være tryg ved. Det var tilstanden af soldaternes støvler. Mere end halvdelen af mændenes støvler var i stykker. Men denne mangel skyldtes ikke regimentschefens forsømmelse, for trods gentagne krav var støvler ikke blevet leveret af det østrigske kommissariat, og regimentet havde marscheret omkring syv hundrede verst.

Regimentschefen var en ældre, kolerisk, svær og firskåren general med gråsprængte øjenbryn og bakkenbarter, bredere fra bryst til ryg end over skuldrene. Han bar en splinterny uniform, der viste folderne fra den kasse, den havde ligget i, og tykke guldepauletter, der syntes at stå op snarere end ligge ned på hans massive skuldre. Han havde minen af en mand, der lykkeligt udfører en af livets mest højtidelige pligter. Han gik frem og tilbage foran linjen og rettede sig op ved hvert skridt, mens han let svajede i ryggen. Det var tydeligt, at han beundrede sit regiment, glædede sig over det, og at hele hans sind var optaget af det, men alligevel syntes hans struttende gang at antyde, at foruden militære sager optog selskabeligt liv og det smukke køn en ikke ringe del af hans tanker.

»Nå, Mikhail Mitritj, hr. oberstløjtnant?« sagde han og henvendte sig til en af bataljonscheferne, der smilende trådte frem (det var tydeligt, at de begge var i godt humør). »Vi havde nok at se til i nat. Men jeg synes, regimentet er ikke så ringe, hvad?«
Bataljonschefen forstod den spøgefulde ironi og lo.
»Det ville ikke blive jaget væk selv fra Tsaritsyn-sletten.«
»Hvad?« spurgte regimentschefen.
I det øjeblik dukkede to mænd til hest op på vejen fra byen, hvor der var posteret signalfolk. Det var en adjudant fulgt af en kosak.

Adjudanten var sendt for at bekræfte den ordre, der dagen før ikke var klart formuleret, nemlig at den øverstbefalende ønskede at se regimentet nøjagtig i den tilstand, det var på marchen: i kapper og med oppakning, uden nogen som helst forberedelse.

Et medlem af Hofkriegsrath i Wien var dagen før kommet til Kutuzov med forslag og krav om at forene sig med ærkehertugen Ferdinand og Macks hær, og Kutuzov, der ikke fandt denne sammenslutning tilrådelig, ville blandt andre argumenter vise den østrigske general den elendige tilstand, tropperne ankom i fra Rusland. Med det formål agtede han at møde regimentet; jo værre tilstand det var i, des mere tilfreds ville den øverstbefalende være. Selvom adjudanten ikke kendte disse omstændigheder, overbragte han dog den bestemte ordre om, at mændene skulle være i kapper og marchuniform, og at den øverstbefalende ellers ville være utilfreds. Da regimentschefen hørte dette, sænkede han hovedet, trak tavst på skuldrene og bredte armene ud med en kolerisk gestus.
»Så har vi da lavet et pænt roderi!« bemærkede han.

»Der kan man bare se! Sagde jeg det ikke, Mikhail Mitritj — når der stod 'på marchen', så mente de i kapperne?« sagde han bebrejdende til bataljonschefen. »Åh, du milde!« tilføjede han og trådte resolut frem. »Kompagnichefer!« råbte han med en stemme, der var vant til at kommandere. »Overfeldwebler! ... Hvornår er han her?« spurgte han adjudanten med en ærbødig høflighed, der tydeligvis gjaldt den person, han omtalte.
»Om en times tid, vil jeg mene.«
»Når vi at skifte?«
»Det ved jeg ikke, hr. general ...«

Regimentschefen gik selv hen til linjen og beordrede soldaterne til at skifte til deres kapper. Kompagnicheferne løb til deres kompagnier, overfeldweblerne begyndte at rave (kapperne var ikke i den bedste forfatning), og øjeblikkeligt begyndte de karréer, der indtil da havde stået i regelmæssig orden og stilhed, at svaje og strække sig og summe af stemmer. Overalt løb soldater til og fra, kastede tornistrene op med et ryk af skuldrene og trak remmene over hovedet, spændte kapperne løs og trak ærmerne på med løftede arme.
I løbet af en halv time var alt igen i orden, blot var karréerne blevet grå i stedet for sorte. Regimentschefen gik med sine rykvis skridt frem foran regimentet og betragtede det på afstand.
»Hvad er det! Det dér!« råbte han og standsede. »Chef for tredje kompagni!«
»Chef for tredje kompagni ønskes af generalen! ... chefen til generalen ... tredje kompagni til chefen.« Ordene fløj ned langs rækkerne, og en adjudant løb for at finde den savnede officer.

Da de ivrige, men forkert gentagne ord havde nået deres mål i et råb: »Generalen til tredje kompagni,« dukkede den savnede officer op bag sit kompagni, og skønt han var en midaldrende mand, der ikke plejede at løbe, travede han akavet og snublende på tåspidserne hen mod generalen. Kaptajnens ansigt viste den uro, en skoledreng føler, når han skal gentage en lektie, han ikke har lært. Pletter viste sig på hans næse, hvis rødme tydeligt skyldtes drikkeri, og munden trak nervøst. Generalen så kaptajnen op og ned, da han kom forpustet hen og sænkede farten ved sin tilnærmelse.

»De klæder snart jeres folk i underkjoler! Hvad er det?« råbte regimentschefen og skød underkæben frem, mens han pegede på en soldat i tredje kompagnis rækker, der bar en kappe af blåligt klæde, som skilte sig ud fra de andres. »Hvad har De lavet? Den øverstbefalende ventes, og De forlader Deres post? Hva? Jeg skal lære Dem at klæde folkene i modekapper til en parade .... Hva? ...«
Kompagnichefen, med øjnene stift rettet mod sin foresatte, pressede to fingre hårdere og hårdere mod kasketten, som om al hans frelse lå i dette tryk.
»Nå, hvorfor siger De ikke noget? Hvem har De fået klædt ud som ungarer dér?« sagde regimentschefen med en streng spøg.
»Deres Eksellence ...«
»Ja, Deres Eksellence, hvad? Deres Eksellence! Men hvad med Deres Eksellence? ... det ved ingen.«
»Deres Eksellence, det er officeren Dolokhov, der er degraderet til menig,« sagde kaptajnen dæmpet.
»Nå? Er han degraderet til feltmarskal eller til soldat? Hvis soldat, skal han bære reglementeret uniform som de andre.«
»Deres Eksellence, De gav ham selv tilladelse på marchen.«

»Gav tilladelse? Tilladelse? Det er typisk jer unge mennesker,« sagde regimentschefen, der kølede lidt af. »Tilladelse, jo tak .... Man siger ét ord til jer, og I ... Hvad?« tilføjede han med fornyet irritation. »Vær venlig at klæde Deres folk ordentligt.«

Og regimentschefen vendte sig for at se på adjudanten og dirigerede sine rykvis skridt ned langs linjen. Han var tydeligvis tilfreds med sit eget vredesudbrud, og da han gik langs regimentet, ledte han efter et nyt påskud for at rase. Han snappede ad en officer for et upoleret emblem, ad en anden, fordi linjen ikke var lige, og nåede frem til tredje kompagni.
»Hvordan stå-å-å-år du? Hvor er dit ben? Dit ben?« råbte regimentschefen med en lidende tone i stemmen, skønt der endnu var fem mand mellem ham og Dolokhov i den blågrå uniform.
Dolokhov rettede langsomt sit bøjede knæ og kiggede lige ind i generalens ansigt med sit klare, frække blik.
»Hvorfor en blå kappe? Af med den ... Overfeldwebel! Skift hans kappe ... den ras...« han fuldførte ikke.
»General, jeg er forpligtet til at adlyde ordrer, men jeg er ikke forpligtet til at finde mig i ...« faldt Dolokhov hurtigt ind.
»Ingen snak i geleddet! ... Ingen snak, ingen snak!«
»Ikke forpligtet til at finde mig i fornærmelser,« afsluttede Dolokhov med høj, klingende stemme.
Generalens og soldatens øjne mødtes. Generalen blev tavs og trak irritabelt sit stramme tørklæde ned.
»Vær så venlig at skifte Deres kappe,« sagde han, idet han vendte sig bort.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: In October 1805, a Russian army was occupying the villages and towns of the Archduchy of Austria, while fresh regiments still arriving from Russia were settling around the fortress of Braunau and burdening the local residents on whom they were billeted. Braunau served as the headquarters of the commander in chief, Kutuzov.

On October 11, 1805, one of the infantry regiments that had just reached Braunau was halted half a mile from town, waiting to be inspected by the commander in chief. Despite the distinctly un-Russian landscape — fruit orchards, stone fences, tiled roofs, and hills in the distance — and despite the fact that the curious locals staring at the soldiers were not Russian, the regiment looked exactly like any Russian regiment preparing for inspection anywhere in the heart of Russia.

The evening before, an order had come down that the commander in chief would inspect the regiment while on the march. Although the wording was unclear to the regimental commander — there was some question about whether the troops should be in marching order or not — a conference of battalion commanders decided to present the regiment in full parade formation, on the principle that it's always better to bow too low than not low enough. So after a twenty-mile march, the soldiers were kept up all night mending and polishing without a moment's sleep, while adjutants and company commanders calculated and recounted, and by morning the regiment — instead of the straggling, disorderly mob it had been on its march the day before — presented a well-ordered display of two thousand men, each of whom knew his place and his duty, with every button and every strap in position, shining with cleanliness. And not only was the exterior in order; had the commander in chief cared to look beneath the uniforms, he would have found a clean shirt on every man and in every knapsack the regulation number of articles — "needle, soap, and all," as the soldiers liked to say. There was only one problem no one could solve: the state of the men's boots. More than half were full of holes. But this wasn't the regimental commander's fault — he had submitted repeated requests, and the Austrian commissariat had simply never delivered the boots. The regiment had marched some seven hundred miles.

The regimental commander was an elderly, hot-tempered, heavyset general with grizzled eyebrows and whiskers, broader from chest to back than across the shoulders. He wore a brand-new uniform still showing its fold creases and thick gold epaulettes that seemed to stand up rather than lie flat on his massive shoulders. He had the air of a man happily performing one of the most solemn duties of his life. He walked back and forth in front of the ranks, pulling himself up and slightly arching his back at every step. It was clear the commander adored his regiment, took immense pride in it, and thought of nothing else — yet his strutting walk also suggested that military matters were not the only thing on his mind, and that social life and the fair sex occupied no small corner of his thoughts.

"Well, Mikhail Mitrich, sir?" he said, addressing one of the battalion commanders, who pressed forward with a smile. It was obvious they were both in high spirits. "We had our hands full last night. Still, I'd say the regiment doesn't look half bad, eh?"
The battalion commander caught the good-humored irony and laughed.
"It wouldn't be turned off the field even on the Tsaritsin parade ground."
"What's that?" asked the commander.
At that moment, two horsemen appeared on the road from town, where lookouts had been posted. They were an aide-de-camp and a Cossack riding behind him.

The aide-de-camp had been sent to clarify the previous day's ambiguously worded order: the commander in chief wanted to see the regiment exactly as it had been on the march — in greatcoats and packs, without any preparation whatsoever.

An official from the Hofkriegsrath in Vienna had visited Kutuzov the previous day with proposals and demands that he join forces with the army of Archduke Ferdinand and Mack. Kutuzov, who considered this merger inadvisable, intended — among other arguments in support of his position — to show the Austrian general the wretched condition in which the troops arrived from Russia. For this purpose he wanted to meet the regiment in its actual state; the worse it looked, the happier the commander in chief would be. Though the aide-de-camp didn't know these background details, he delivered the definite order: the men were to be in greatcoats and marching order, and the commander in chief would be displeased otherwise. Hearing this, the regimental commander hung his head, shrugged silently, and threw out his arms in frustration.
"A fine mess we've made of it!" he said.

"Didn't I tell you, Mikhail Mitrich? When they said 'on the march,' it meant in greatcoats!" he said reproachfully to the battalion commander. "Oh, my God!" He stepped forward decisively. "Company commanders!" he bellowed in a voice built for commanding. "Sergeants major!... How soon will he be here?" he asked the aide-de-camp with a respectful politeness clearly directed at the personage in question.
"An hour, I'd say."
"Will we have time to change?"
"I couldn't say, General."

The regimental commander walked up to the line himself and ordered the soldiers to change into their greatcoats. Company commanders ran to their companies, sergeants major began scrambling — the greatcoats weren't in the best shape — and instantly the silent, orderly squares began to sway, stretch, and buzz with voices. Soldiers ran in every direction, tossing their knapsacks up with a jerk of the shoulders, pulling straps over their heads, unbuckling overcoats and jamming their arms through the sleeves.

Within half an hour, everything was back in order — only the squares had turned from black to gray. The regimental commander walked with his jerky steps to the front and surveyed the whole formation from a distance.
"What in the — what is this? This!" he shouted, stopping short. "Commander of the third company!"

"Commander of the third company — the general wants you!... Commander to the general... third company to the commander!" The words passed down the lines, and an adjutant ran off to find the missing officer.

When the eager but garbled message finally reached its destination as "The general to the third company!" the missing officer appeared from behind his men and — though he was a middle-aged man not accustomed to running — came trotting awkwardly toward the general, stumbling on his toes. The captain's face wore the anxious look of a schoolboy called on to recite a lesson he hasn't learned. Spots bloomed on his nose, whose redness was clearly the result of heavy drinking, and his mouth twitched nervously. The general looked him up and down as he arrived, panting and slowing his pace.

"You'll be dressing your men in petticoats next! What is this?" the regimental commander barked, jutting his jaw toward a soldier in the third company's ranks who wore a greatcoat of bluish cloth that stood out from all the others. "What have you been doing? The commander in chief is about to arrive and you abandon your post? I'll teach you to put fancy coats on your men for inspection!"
The company commander pressed two fingers ever harder to his cap visor, as if all his salvation lay in that gesture.
"Well? Why don't you answer? Who's that you've got dressed up like a Hungarian?" the commander demanded with grim sarcasm.
"Your excellency..."
"Well? 'Your excellency' what? 'Your excellency'! Nobody seems to know anything around here."
"Your excellency, it's the officer Dolokhov, who was reduced to the ranks," the captain said quietly.
"So? Has he been demoted to field marshal, or to private? If he's a private, he wears regulation uniform like everyone else."
"Your excellency, you gave him permission yourself, on the march."

"Permission? Permission? That's just like you young officers," the regimental commander said, cooling off slightly. "Permission, indeed... You say one word to any of you and then... What?" he added, his irritation flaring again. "I'm asking you to dress your men properly."

He turned to the adjutant and continued down the line with his jerky stride. He was clearly enjoying his own display of anger and looking for another target. Having snapped at one officer over an unpolished badge and at another for a crooked line, he reached the third company.
"How are you standing? Where's your leg? Your leg!" the commander bellowed in a pained voice, though he was still five men away from Dolokhov in his bluish-gray coat.
Dolokhov slowly straightened his bent knee, staring directly at the general's face with clear, insolent eyes.
"Why a blue coat? Take it off... Sergeant major! Change his coat — the ras—" He didn't finish.
"General, I must follow orders, but I am not required to endure —" Dolokhov cut in sharply.
"No talking in the ranks! No talking!"
"— insults," Dolokhov finished, his voice loud, clear, and ringing.
The general's eyes met the soldier's. The general fell silent, tugging angrily at his tight collar.
"I would ask you to kindly change your coat," he said as he turned and walked away.
